question: Which of these best describes an algorithm?
correct: A finite list of unambiguous steps that solves a problem
incorrect: Any program, as long as it compiles and runs without errors
A routine for searching or sorting, the two jobs algorithms do
A diagram of boxes and arrows showing how a program flows
feedback: An algorithm is the plan, not the program: a limited number of steps, each clear enough that nobody has to guess what it means. A program is one way of writing an algorithm down and a flowchart is one way of drawing it, but a recipe or a set of directions can be an algorithm too. Searching and sorting are famous examples, not the definition.

question: Which of these are properties an algorithm must have?
correct: Definiteness: each step is precise, with no room for interpretation
Finiteness: it stops after a limited number of steps
Effectiveness: each step is basic enough to actually carry out
Input and output: it takes defined inputs and produces a result
incorrect: Efficiency: it uses the fewest steps possible for the problem
Language: it is written in a programming language such as Java
feedback: Definite, finite, effective, with inputs and an output: those four make something an algorithm. Efficiency is what makes one algorithm better than another, not what makes it an algorithm; a slow linear search is still an algorithm. And an algorithm exists before any code does: it can be written in pseudocode, drawn as a flowchart, or spoken aloud.

question: Match each flowchart symbol to what it stands for.

pairs.definition: The start or the end of the whole process
An action or calculation, such as total = total + 1
A yes/no question with two paths leading out

feedback: Ovals mark where the process starts and ends, rectangles do the work, parallelograms move data in or out, and arrows give the order. The diamond is the only shape with two ways out, which is why every if and every loop test in a flowchart is drawn as one.

question: In a flowchart, a diamond asks  n > 0?  Its Yes arrow leads to a rectangle holding  n = n - 1, and an arrow from that rectangle leads back up to the diamond. Its No arrow leads on to End. Which Java construct does this shape describe?
incorrect: An if statement
An if-else statement
A do-while loop
feedback: An arrow that travels back to an earlier diamond is what makes a loop; an if or if-else only ever flows forward. The question is asked before the rectangle runs, so the body might run zero times: that is a while loop. A do-while would be drawn with the rectangle first and the diamond underneath it.

question:
Trace this pseudocode. What number does it display?
SET total TO 0
SET n TO {{a}}
WHILE n > 0
    ADD n TO total
    SUBTRACT {{s}} FROM n
END WHILE
DISPLAY total
feedback_template: n starts at {{a}} and drops by {{s}} on every pass. Each value of n that is still above 0 is added to total, and those values add up to {{expected}}. The test sits at the top of the loop, so once n reaches 0 or less nothing more is added. Keeping a two-column table (n, total) is the reliable way to trace it.

question: Arrange this pseudocode, first step to last, so that it displays the average of a list of scores.
items: FOR EACH score IN scores: ADD score TO total
SET average TO total / NUMBER OF scores
feedback: Each step needs the one before it: total must exist before anything is added to it, the division is only meaningful once every score is in, and there is nothing to display until average has been computed. Pseudocode lets you settle that order before worrying about Java's syntax.

feedback_template: total holds {{s}} before the loop, and each pass adds one element to it, so it ends at {{expected}}. Whatever the accumulator holds before the loop is part of the answer. That is why a sum is normally started at 0, the one value that adds nothing.

prompt: Fill in the starting values and the counter's update so that all three results come out right.
feedback: Start every accumulator at the value that changes nothing: 1 for a product (starting at 0 would make every product 0), 0 for a counter, false for a flag that flips to true when the target is seen. A counter goes up by exactly one for each element that passes the test, whatever that element's value is.

feedback_template: continue abandons the rest of the body for that one pass only: i++ still runs and the loop carries on. So the multiples of {{k}} between 1 and {{n}} are skipped, and the other {{expected}} values of i reach count++. This is a counter with a filter in front of it.

question: Which statements about accumulator loops are correct?
correct: Writing  total = 0;  inside the loop body wipes the running total on every pass
One loop can keep a sum and a counter going at the same time
incorrect: An accumulator declared inside the loop body can still be printed after the loop
A local int that is given no starting value begins at 0 on its own
The update  total = v;  does the same job as  total += v;
feedback: The accumulator has to be declared and given its starting value before the loop. Reset it inside and only the last element survives; declare it inside and it no longer exists after the closing brace (the compiler reports it cannot find the symbol). Java also refuses to read a local variable that was never assigned, rather than quietly using 0. And  total = v  replaces the total where  total += v  adds to it. One pass over the data can feed as many accumulators as you like, which is how an average gets its sum and its count.

question: NPC: The maximum that was never in the array
intro: Nia unrolls a miner's log of depth readings, every one below zero. “Find me the largest reading,” she says. “I will do it the way most apprentices do first.”

steps.say: max is just a variable that remembers the largest element met so far. I start it at 0 and let every element challenge it.

beats.say: max is just a variable that remembers the largest element met so far. I started it at 0, and each element challenges it in turn.

steps.say: Trace it. Is -4 greater than 0? No. Is -9? No. Is -2? No. The if never succeeds.

check.prompt: So what does the program print?
check.why: No element ever beat 0, so max was never updated. It prints 0, a number that is not even in the array.

steps.say: The repair: start max from a real element, the first one. Then -9 fails to beat -4, -2 does beat it, and the answer is -2.

beats.say: The starting value was the bug: 0 was my invention, not a reading. The repair is to start from a real element, the first one.
Now max begins at -4. -9 fails to beat it, -2 does beat it, and the program prints -2. The same rule holds for a minimum: start from an element of the array, never from a number you made up.

outro: “The next monster made the same mistake while hunting for a minimum. Trace what its code really prints.”

question: This code is meant to find the lowest temperature. Trace it: what does it actually print?
feedback: 12, 7 and 9 are all larger than 0, so the if never succeeds and min keeps its made-up starting value. The output, 0, is not even an element of the array. Starting with  int min = temps[0];  fixes it: then 7 replaces 12, 9 fails to replace 7, and the code prints 7.

question: A loop is finding the largest value in an int array a, remembering it in a variable named max. The test  if (a[i] > max)  has just come out true. Write the one statement that belongs inside that if.
feedback: When the current element beats the best so far, it becomes the new best: max = a[i];  The assignment copies right to left, so writing a[i] = max; would overwrite the array with the old maximum instead of remembering the new one.

question: This loop remembers a position rather than a value. What does it print?
feedback: minIdx starts at 0 (value 14). Index 1 holds 6, which is smaller, so minIdx becomes 1. 11 is not smaller than 6. Index 3 holds 2, which is smaller, so minIdx becomes 3. 8 is not smaller than 2. It prints the position and then the value: 3 2. Tracking the index is what a sort needs, because it must know where the smallest element is in order to move it.

question: An apprentice tries to swap two variables. What does this print?
feedback: a = b; overwrites the 4 with 9, and from that moment the 4 is gone. b = a; then copies 9 back into b. Both variables end up holding 9. A swap needs a third variable to keep the first value safe while it is being overwritten.

prompt: Complete the swap of a[i] and a[j] so that neither value is lost.
feedback: tmp keeps a copy of a[i], so a[i] can safely be overwritten with a[j]. The old a[i] now survives only in tmp, so that is what goes into a[j]. Writing a[j] = a[i]; on the last line would copy the new value back and leave both slots the same.

question: The search code written in this course reports the index where the target was found. Why does it report -1, rather than 0, when the target is absent?
correct: 0 is a real index, so it would be mistaken for a match at the front
incorrect: -1 is what Java stores in an int that was never assigned
0 would stop the loop before the last element is checked
-1 is the index just past the end of any array
feedback: The answer is an index, and every index from 0 to length - 1 means 'found here', so 'not found' needs a value that can never be an index. -1 is the usual choice, and String's indexOf makes the same one. It is a convention, not something Java supplies: the code has to set it. (The library's own Arrays.binarySearch reports a miss with other negative numbers, so test for < 0 rather than == -1 there.)

question: A linear search checks an array of {{n}} elements from index 0 upward and stops as soon as it meets the target, which is sitting at index {{k}}. How many elements did it compare with the target?
feedback_template: Indexes start at 0, so reaching index {{k}} means indexes 0 through {{k}} were all compared: {{expected}} elements. The rest of the {{n}} are never looked at, which is what stopping early buys. Had the target been absent, all {{n}} would have been compared.

question: The target appears more than once in this array. What does the search print?
feedback: Nothing stops this loop once it has a match, so it keeps going and idx is overwritten at index 0, again at index 2, and finally at index 4. It reports the LAST match. Adding break; after idx = i; would leave the loop at the first match and print 0, and would save the wasted comparisons as well.

question: This binary search is run on an array that is NOT in sorted order. The target 9 is in the array. What does it print?
feedback: The first probe is index 2, which holds 7. Since 7 < 9 the code throws away indexes 0 to 2, and the 9 at index 0 goes with them. The later probes (4, then 1) fail too, and idx stays -1. Binary search never looks at most of the array; it trusts the ordering to tell it where the target cannot be. On unsorted data that trust is misplaced, and it gives wrong answers without any error message.

question: NPC: Three markers on a sorted shelf
intro: Seven numbered scrolls sit in order on a shelf. Nia sets three brass markers beside them, labelled lo, mid and hi. “Binary search is nothing more than moving these three,” she says.

steps.say: lo and hi fence in the part of the array where the target could still be. mid is the index halfway between them, and it is the only element I examine: one probe.

beats.say: I am hunting for 23 in a sorted array:
lo and hi fence in the indexes where the target could still be. mid is the index halfway between them, and nums[mid] is the only element I examine. That is one probe: nums[3] is 12.

steps.say: 12 is smaller than 23, and the array is sorted.

check.prompt: 12 is smaller than 23, and the array is sorted. Which indexes can still hold 23?
check.why: Everything left of index 3 is even smaller than 12, and index 3 itself has just been examined, so lo jumps to mid + 1 = 4.

steps.say: Second probe: mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, and nums[5] is 23. Found in two probes. Each probe halves what is left, so the worst case is: halve the size until 1 element remains, then add one probe for that last element. 7, 3, 1 is two halvings, so 3 probes at most.

beats.say: Second probe: lo is 4 and hi is 6, so mid is 5, and nums[5] is 23. Found, in two probes.

Each probe throws away half of what is left. To get the worst case, halve the size (dropping fractions) until 1 element remains, then add one probe for that last element. For 7 elements: 7, 3, 1 is two halvings, so 3 probes at most.

outro: “The next monster's search prints mid on every pass. Move the markers yourself and write down each mid.”

question: This binary search prints mid on every pass. What is its complete output?
feedback: Pass 1: lo 0, hi 8, mid 4; nums[4] is 21, too big, so hi becomes 3. Pass 2: mid is (0 + 3) / 2 = 1 by int division; nums[1] is 6, too small, so lo becomes 2. Pass 3: mid is (2 + 3) / 2 = 2; nums[2] is 10, found. Three probes for nine elements, where a linear search would also have needed three here but could need nine.

question:
Partway through a binary search, lo is {{lo}} and hi is {{hi}}. What value does this statement store?
int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
feedback_template: lo + hi is {{total}}, and dividing one int by another drops any fraction, so mid is {{expected}}. When the sum is odd there is no exact middle, and the search simply probes the lower of the two middle indexes.

question: In a binary search loop that runs  while (lo <= hi), an apprentice writes  lo = mid;  where the standard code has  lo = mid + 1;  What is the risk?
correct: The range can stop shrinking, so the loop may never end
incorrect: The element at mid is skipped and can never be found
The search still works but needs about twice the probes
mid can pass hi and index beyond the end of the array
feedback: Suppose lo is 4 and hi is 5. mid is (4 + 5) / 2 = 4, and if nums[4] is too small, lo = mid sets lo to 4 again: nothing changed, so the next pass is identical, forever. The + 1 is safe because index mid has just been examined and ruled out, and it guarantees the range shrinks on every pass. mid always lies between lo and hi, so it cannot run off the array.

question: A sorted array holds {{n}} elements. In the worst case, how many elements does a standard binary search examine before it can stop?
feedback_template: Each probe discards at least half of what is left. {{n}} can be halved (dropping fractions) {{halvings}} times before only 1 element remains, and that last element still has to be examined: {{expected}} probes. Watch the exact powers of 2: 1,000 elements need 10 probes at most, but 1,024 need 11.

question: Each probe of a binary search halves what is left to search, so doubling the array adds just one probe. In Big-O notation, with n elements, its worst case is written O(___).
feedback: The number of times n can be halved before reaching 1 is its base-2 logarithm, so binary search is O(log n). Big-O ignores the base and any small constant, which is why log n, log₂ n and lg n all name the same growth rate. Compare linear search's O(n): at a million elements that is about 20 probes against a possible 1,000,000.

question: Which statements about linear search and binary search are correct?
correct: Linear search gives the right answer on an array in any order
Binary search of 1,000 sorted elements needs at most 10 probes
For one lookup in a small unsorted array, linear search is the sensible choice
incorrect: Linear search has to examine every element even after it has met the target
Sorting the array first lowers linear search's worst-case number of comparisons
feedback: Linear search assumes nothing about order, and it can stop the moment it finds the target. Its worst case is a target that is absent, which costs n comparisons whether or not the data is sorted. Binary search is far faster on big sorted arrays (1,000 halves down to 1 in 9 steps, plus one last probe), but sorting just to do a single lookup costs more than the linear search it replaces.

question: NPC: Selection sort, one pass at a time
intro: Nia lays four numbered tiles in a row: 5, 2, 8, 1. “Sorting by hand,” she says. “One rule, repeated. Watch what a single pass does.”

steps.say: A pass of selection sort finds the smallest value in the unsorted part and swaps it into the first unsorted index.

beats.say: One pass of selection sort does two things: it finds the smallest value in the unsorted part, then swaps it into the first unsorted index.
Pass 1: the unsorted part is everything. The smallest value is 1, at index 3, so I swap index 3 with index 0. The array is now 1 2 8 5, and index 0 is finished for good.

steps.say: Pass 2 looks only at indexes 1 to 3, which hold 2, 8 and 5.

check.prompt: Pass 2 looks only at indexes 1 to 3, which hold 2, 8 and 5. What does it do?
check.answer: Finds 2 already at index 1, so nothing moves
check.why: The smallest of 2, 8, 5 is the 2, and it is already sitting at index 1, the first unsorted index. It swaps with itself and the array still reads 1 2 8 5.

steps.say: Pass 3 looks at indexes 2 to 3: the smallest is 5, so it swaps with the 8, giving 1 2 5 8. Four elements needed three passes, because the last element has nowhere else to go.

beats.say: Pass 3 looks at indexes 2 to 3, holding 8 and 5. The smallest is the 5, so it swaps with the 8: 1 2 5 8.
Four elements needed only three passes, because once all the others are placed the last one has nowhere else to go. After pass number k, the first k indexes hold their final values.

outro: “Now the code version. A monster ahead runs exactly one pass on a different array. Find the smallest, then swap.”

question: This is the first pass of selection sort. What does it print?
feedback: The loop finds the smallest value, 2, at index 3. The three-line swap then exchanges a[0] and a[3], so the 7 goes to where the 2 was: 2 4 9 7 6. Only two elements move in a pass; the 4, 9 and 6 stay exactly where they were, even though they are not yet in order.

question: Selection sort (smallest first) runs on the array 6 9 2 8 1. Put the states of the array in order, from the starting array to the array after pass 3.
feedback: Pass 1 swaps the smallest value, 1, with whatever is at index 0 (the 6). Pass 2 searches indexes 1 to 4, finds 2, and swaps it with the 9. Pass 3 searches indexes 2 to 4, finds 6, and swaps it with the 9. Each pass fixes exactly one more index at the front, and each swap can send a large value a long way back.

question: Arrange these lines, top to bottom, into the body of one selection-sort pass: it must move the smallest value found from index i onward into index i.
items: for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++)
feedback: minIdx has to exist before the inner loop can update it, and the if is the body of that for. The swap can only begin once the loop has finished, because until then minIdx is not yet the position of the smallest value. Inside the swap, tmp saves a[minIdx] first, so that slot can be overwritten with a[i], and the saved value goes into a[i] last.

question: Selection sort (smallest first) has completed 3 passes over an array of 10 different values. What is certain about the array at that moment?
correct: Indexes 0 to 2 hold the three smallest values, already in their final order
incorrect: Indexes 7 to 9 hold the three largest values, in their final order
Indexes 0 to 2 are in order, but smaller values may lie further right
Every value has been moved at least once toward its final index
feedback: Each pass selects the smallest value remaining and swaps it into the next index at the front, so after 3 passes indexes 0 to 2 are finished and will never be touched again. A sort that fixes the largest values at the back first is bubble sort; one whose front part is in order but not yet final is insertion sort. And selection sort moves at most two values per pass, so most values may not have moved at all.

feedback_template: On the first pass j runs from 1 to the last index, which is {{first}} comparisons. Every later pass starts j one place further along, so it makes one fewer, down to a single comparison on the last pass. Adding {{first}} and every whole number below it gives {{expected}}. The count is the same whatever order the values are in: selection sort cannot finish early.

question: Selection sort is being adapted for a String[] named a. The test  a[j] < a[m]  does not compile, because < does not work on Strings. Which replacement is correct?
incorrect: a[j].compareTo(a[m]) == -1
a[j].equals(a[m]) < 0
a[j].compareTo(a[m]) == true
feedback: compareTo answers with an int: negative when the first String comes earlier in dictionary order, zero when they match, positive when it comes later. The negative number is not promised to be -1 ("pear".compareTo("plum") is -7), so always test < 0. equals gives back a boolean, which can only say same-or-different, never which comes first. The order is by character code, so every capital letter sorts ahead of every lowercase one: "Zebra" comes before "apple".

question: Real programs rarely sort by hand. With java.util.Arrays imported, what does this print?
feedback: Arrays.sort rearranges the array itself into ascending order, giving 5 8 17 23 40, so the first element is the smallest and the last is the largest. It hands nothing back; the original order is gone. The library's sort is far faster than selection sort on large arrays, so you trace selection sort to understand sorting and call Arrays.sort to get work done.

question: Each fragment works on an int array a of length n. Match it to how its running time grows.

pairs.definition: Constant: the same work however large n is

pairs.term: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];
pairs.definition: Linear: doubling n doubles the work

pairs.term: for (int i = n; i > 1; i = i / 2) steps++;
pairs.definition: Logarithmic: doubling n adds a single step
Quadratic: doubling n makes four times the work

feedback: Count how often the innermost statement runs. One array access is one step whatever n is. A single loop over the array runs n times. A loop that halves i reaches 1 after about log₂ n passes, so even a huge n costs only a handful of steps. A full loop nested in another runs n × n times, the pattern behind selection sort and the reason it struggles on big arrays.

question: For an unsorted int array of n elements, which of these jobs take time that grows in proportion to n (linear time)?
correct: Linear search for a value that turns out to be absent
incorrect: Sorting the array with selection sort
Reading the last element, a[n - 1]
Swapping the first element with the last
feedback: Summing, finding the maximum and an unsuccessful linear search each visit every element once: n steps, so linear. Selection sort runs a loop inside a loop and needs roughly n × n / 2 comparisons, which is quadratic. Reading a[n - 1] and the three-line swap each take the same few steps whether the array has ten elements or ten million: constant time.

question: A shop's array of 100,000 item codes is unsorted, never changes, and will be searched thousands of times a day. Which plan does the least total work?
correct: Sort it once, then use binary search for every lookup after that
incorrect: Use linear search every time, since sorting costs more than it saves
Use binary search straight away, since it needs so few probes
Sort it before each lookup, then use binary search on the result
feedback: Binary search on unsorted data gives wrong answers, so it cannot simply be used straight away. Sorting is expensive, but here the cost is paid once and then shared by thousands of lookups of about 17 probes each, instead of up to 100,000 comparisons each. Sorting again before every lookup throws that saving away. If the array were only going to be searched once, plain linear search would win.

question: The target is not in this sorted array. What does the search print?
feedback: Pass 1: mid is (0 + 7) / 2 = 3; 20 is too small, so lo becomes 4. Pass 2: mid is (4 + 7) / 2 = 5; 31 is too big, so hi becomes 4. Pass 3: mid is 4; 26 is too small, so lo becomes 5. Now lo (5) is greater than hi (4): the fenced-in range is empty, the loop ends, and idx still holds -1. A miss is detected when lo and hi cross, after only 3 of the 8 elements were examined.
